pos: n. (elder son of Isaac and twin of Jacob, father of Edom — the profane man who sold a birthright for a meal, and the Bible's standing case of reprobation)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Esav, probably “hairy” or “rough”, from his appearance at birth. He is also called 'Edom, red, from the red pottage he traded for, and from that name comes the nation of Edom in mount Seir.
biblical_def: Esau was born first, red and hairy, with his brother's hand on his heel, and the oracle over the womb had already settled the order: “the elder shall serve the younger” (Gen 25:23). He was a cunning hunter and his father's favourite, and he was, by his own act, a profane man. Coming in faint from the field he traded the birthright — the double portion and the covenant headship of the house of Abraham — for a bowl of lentils, and the writer's judgment is savage in its brevity: “he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright” (Gen 25:34). Years later, cheated of the blessing as well, he broke: “Hast thou but one blessing, my father? bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept” (Gen 27:38). Hebrews reads that scene exactly: he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears (Heb 12:17) — he wanted the inheritance back, not the sin undone. And yet Scripture will not flatten him into a monster. Twenty years on he came out with four hundred men and did the unexpected thing: “Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept” (Gen 33:4). Common grace, real affection, and no covenant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Esau; in sacred history he is the elder son of Isaac and Rebekah, twin brother of Jacob, and father of the Edomites.
webster_full: ESAU, n. The elder son of Isaac, born red and hairy, whence his name; also called Edom.
He was a cunning hunter, and a man of the field, and his father loved him.
He sold his birthright unto Jacob for a mess of pottage.
Being deprived also of the blessing, he purposed in his heart to slay his brother, but was afterward reconciled to him.
He dwelt in mount Seir, and became the father of the Edomites.
scriptures: Then Jacob gave Esau bread and pottage of lentiles; and he did eat and drink, and rose up, and went his way: thus Esau despised his birthright.
And Esau said unto his father, Hast thou but one blessing, my father? bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.
Gen 33:4
And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept.
Rom 9:13
As it is written, Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated.
corruption_summary: Rom 9:13 is softened into a statement about nations, or about foreseen character, to escape the doctrine Paul is actually defending — that election rests on God's purpose and not on the man.
corruption_paragraphs: “Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated” is the verse the modern reader most wants to dilute, and two dilutions are standard. The first says Malachi speaks of the nations Israel and Edom, not the men. The second says God foresaw Esau's profanity and elected accordingly. Paul forecloses both in advance, and it is worth watching him do it. He specifies twins, one father, one mother, one conception; and he fixes the timing — the word came “the children being not yet born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand, not of works, but of him that calleth” (Rom 9:11). Foreseen character is the exact thing that clause excludes. Paul then raises the objection himself — “Is there unrighteousness with God?” — which no one would raise against a doctrine about national fortunes. The dictionary holds unconditional election and the justice of reprobation, and holds that the God who hardens is never the author of the sin He justly punishes.

The second corruption is sentimental rather than doctrinal: Esau's tears are read as genuine repentance rejected by a harsh God. Heb 12:17 says he “found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears”, and the sorrow was for the lost estate, not for the despised birthright. Paul names the difference: “godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death” (2Co 7:10). A man may weep bitterly over consequences and never once hate his sin. Esau is the pattern of the profane man in Scripture — not the blasphemer, but the man who holds eternal things cheap when he is hungry.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Esav (H6215), Esau, hairy; 'Edom (H123), red; bekorah (H1062), birthright; Greek bebelos (G952), profane.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Esav (H6215) — Esau; from a root suggesting hairiness or roughness.
Hebrew 'Edom (H123) — Edom, red; the nickname from the red pottage, and the name of his nation.
Hebrew bekorah (H1062) — the birthright; the double portion and the headship of the house.
Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, hold in contempt; the verb of Gen 25:34.
Greek bebelos (G952) — profane, unhallowed; literally what may be trodden, the word Hebrews applies to him.
usage: “Thus Esau despised his birthright” — five words of verdict on a whole life.
“Bless me, even me also, O my father” — grief for the estate, not for the sin.
“Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him” — real kindness outside the covenant.

pos: n. (Syrian captain, leper, and convert — the Gentile healed in Jordan whom the Lord Jesus named to a synagogue that tried to kill Him for it)
etymology: From Hebrew Na'aman, “pleasantness”, from na'em, to be pleasant or agreeable — the same root as Naomi. It is a name of grace on a man who had to be brought very low to receive any.
biblical_def: Naaman is introduced with a string of honours and one word that undoes them all: “captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” (2Ki 5:1). Note who is said to have given Syria its victories. The gospel reaches him by the lowest possible channel — a captive Israelite girl waiting on his wife — and it reaches him crooked, through a king's letter and a diplomatic incident, before Elisha sends a messenger to the door with an order and does not come out himself. Naaman was furious: he had a script in his head about how a prophet should behave, and he had better rivers at home. His servants reasoned with him, and he went down. “Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean” (2Ki 5:14). What follows is a confession: “Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” (2Ki 5:15). He asked for two mules' burden of earth to build an altar on, and asked pardon for the bowing he would still have to do in the house of Rimmon. The Lord Jesus cited him at Nazareth: “none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian” (Luk 4:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Naaman; in sacred history he is the captain of the host of the king of Syria, cleansed of leprosy by washing seven times in Jordan.
webster_full: NAAMAN, n. Captain of the host of Benhadad king of Syria; the name signifies pleasantness.
He was a mighty man of valour, but a leper.
A little captive maid of Israel told her mistress of the prophet in Samaria.
Being sent to Elisha, he was bidden to wash seven times in Jordan, and his flesh came again as the flesh of a little child.
He confessed the God of Israel, and took with him two mules' burden of earth to build an altar.
scriptures: Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.
Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant.
Luk 4:27
And many lepers were in Israel in the time of Eliseus the prophet; and none of them was cleansed, saving Naaman the Syrian.
corruption_summary: Naaman is preached as a lesson in humility and obedience, which he is; what the Lord Jesus made of him is sovereign election running past the covenant people to a foreign soldier.
corruption_paragraphs: Everyone preaches Naaman's pride, and rightly — the great man rehearsing in advance how the prophet ought to come out and wave his hand is one of the most recognisable portraits in Scripture. But the use the Lord Jesus made of the story in the synagogue at Nazareth was different and far more offensive. He said that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's day and not one of them was cleansed — only the Syrian. Israelite lepers by the score, a prophet in the land, and the healing went to a Gentile officer of the army that raided Israel's borders. His hearers, Luke says, were filled with wrath and led Him to the brow of the hill to cast Him down headlong. Sovereign, discriminating mercy is not a doctrine invented by Calvin; it is the doctrine that nearly got the Lord killed before His ministry was a month old.

The other thing usually mishandled is Naaman's last request. He asks pardon for bowing in the house of Rimmon when he supports his master's arm, and Elisha answers, “Go in peace.” Some read this as licence for the believer to conform outwardly in an idolatrous setting; it will not carry that weight, and the three young men before Nebuchadnezzar's image settle the matter for a case of actual worship. What the exchange does show is a new convert with a real conscience about a real difficulty, and a prophet who did not load him with a rule he had not been given. Elisha neither approved the bowing nor pronounced on it; he blessed a man at the beginning of his obedience. Pastors would do well to notice the restraint.
roots_summary: Hebrew Na'aman (H5283), from na'em (H5276), to be pleasant; tsara'ath (H6883), leprosy; taphal / tabal (H2881), to dip.
roots_lines: Hebrew Na'aman (H5283) — Naaman, “pleasantness”; the same root as Naomi.
Hebrew tsara'ath (H6883) — the leprosy of the law; a ceremonial uncleanness that pictured sin's defilement.
Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip, immerse; the verb of the seven washings in Jordan.
Hebrew Rimmon (H7417) — Rimmon, the Syrian thunder-god in whose house Naaman had to attend his master.
Greek Neeman (G3497) — Naaman; named by the Lord Jesus at Nazareth (Luk 4:27).
usage: “A mighty man in valour, but he was a leper” — the sentence that turns on one word.
“His flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child” — cleansing by an ordinary washing.
“There is no God in all the earth, but in Israel” — a Syrian's confession.

pos: n. (the Agagite, chief minister of Ahasuerus — author of the first recorded plan to exterminate the Jews, hanged on his own gallows)
etymology: From Hebrew Haman, probably of Persian origin and connected with the name of the god Humban or with a word for magnificence. He is called ha-'Agagi, the Agagite, which links him to Agag king of Amalek and so to the oldest feud in Israel's history.
biblical_def: Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite was promoted by Ahasuerus above all the princes (Est 3:1) and required that all bow. Mordecai the Jew would not, and the offence metastasised at once from a man to a people: “when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath” (Est 3:5), and “he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone… wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” (Est 3:6). He cast Pur, the lot, for the month; he bought the decree with ten thousand talents of silver; he had it written and sealed with the king's ring and posted to a hundred and twenty-seven provinces. Then the reversals begin, and they are relentless: a sleepless king, a chronicle read aloud, an honour Haman designed for himself and had to bestow on his enemy, a banquet, an accusation, a fall across a couch. “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai” (Est 7:10). The book never once mentions the name of God, and every page of it is His — “his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head” (Est 9:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Haman; in sacred history he is the Agagite favourite of Ahasuerus who sought to destroy the Jews and was hanged on his own gallows.
webster_full: HAMAN, n. The son of Hammedatha the Agagite, chief minister of Ahasuerus king of Persia.
Being enraged that Mordecai would not do him reverence, he obtained a decree for the destruction of all the Jews.
The lot, called Pur, was cast before him to determine the month and the day.
He built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai, and was himself hanged thereon.
The feast of Purim was appointed in memory of the deliverance from his device.
scriptures: Est 3:1
After these things did king Ahasuerus promote Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him, and set his seat above all the princes that were with him.
Est 3:5
And when Haman saw that Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence, then was Haman full of wrath.
Est 3:6

And he thought scorn to lay hands on Mordecai alone; for they had shewed him the people of Mordecai: wherefore Haman sought to destroy all the Jews that were throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, even the people of Mordecai.
Est 7:10
So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.
corruption_summary: Esther is dismissed as a nationalist folk-tale because God is never named in it; the absence is the point — it is the book of hidden providence, where nothing is miraculous and everything is arranged.
corruption_paragraphs: The book of Esther has been treated as a problem since Luther's complaint about it: no name of God, no prayer recorded, no temple, no law, no miracle, and a great deal of blood at the end. Read as folklore it is indefensible. Read as it presents itself, it is the most sustained demonstration in Scripture of ordinary providence — the doctrine that God governs all His creatures and all their actions, including the free wicked ones, without ever suspending a law of nature. A beauty contest, an overheard plot, an insomniac king, a chronicle opened at the right page, a question asked before its object is named, a queen's courage, a lot cast eleven months early to give time for a counter-decree. Not one of these is a miracle and every one of them is arranged. Pro 16:33 gives the hinge of the whole book: “The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.”

The second thing to name is what Haman is. He is the Agagite, and Agag was the Amalekite king Saul spared and Samuel hewed in pieces, and Amalek was the nation that fell on the feeble at the rear of Israel coming out of Egypt, of whom God said He would have war with them from generation to generation. Mordecai is a Benjamite of the house of Kish — Saul's house. The feud Saul left unfinished returns five centuries later with the whole nation in the balance. Sin left half-dealt-with in one generation waits in the next. And the shape of Haman's end is a doctrine on its own: the gallows he built stood ready, and the man who built it hung on it. “Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein” (Pro 26:27).
roots_summary: Hebrew Haman (H2001), of Persian origin; 'Agagi (H91), Agagite; pur (H6332), a lot, whence Purim.
roots_lines: Hebrew Haman (H2001) — Haman; a Persian name, borne by the enemy of the Jews.
Hebrew 'Agagi (H91) — Agagite; linking him to Agag of Amalek (1Sa 15).
Hebrew pur (H6332) — the lot, a Persian loanword glossed in the text itself; hence the feast of Purim.
Hebrew 'ets (H6086) — a tree, gallows, stake; the fifty-cubit structure he raised.
Hebrew shub…'al ro'sho — to return upon his own head; the formula of poetic justice in Est 9:25.
usage: “Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite” — an old feud in a new court.
“Haman sought to destroy all the Jews” — a private slight made national.
“They hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared” — the reversal the book exists for.

pos: n. (younger daughter of Saul and first wife of David — who saved his life through a window and despised him for dancing before the ark)
etymology: From Hebrew Mikal, a shortened form of the question mi ka-'El, “who is like God?” — the same question behind the name Michael. It is a great name, and her story turns on the answer to it.
biblical_def: Michal loved David, and Saul made a weapon of it, demanding a hundred Philistine foreskins for a dowry in hopes David would die getting them. He brought two hundred. When Saul sent men to the house to kill him in the morning, she let him out: “so Michal let David down through a window: and he went, and fled, and escaped” (1Sa 19:12), and put an image in the bed with goats' hair for a pillow and lied to her father's men. Saul then gave her to another man, Phalti, and years later David demanded her back as a term of his treaty with Abner; Phalti followed her weeping to Bahurim and was sent home. The last scene is the famous one. The ark came up to the city of David with shouting and the sound of the trumpet, and the king danced before the LORD with all his might in a linen ephod, and “Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2Sa 6:16). She met him at the door with a sneer about the handmaids (2Sa 6:20); he answered that he would be yet more vile, and would be had in honour by those very maidservants. The chapter closes with a sentence of terrible finality: “Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death” (2Sa 6:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Michal; in sacred history she is the younger daughter of Saul, given to David to wife, who saved him from her father and afterward despised him.
webster_full: MICHAL, n. The younger daughter of Saul, king of Israel; the name signifies who is like God.
She loved David, and was given him to wife for a hundred of the Philistines.
She let him down through a window and deceived the messengers of Saul with an image in the bed.
In David's absence Saul gave her to Phalti the son of Laish, and she was afterward restored.
Despising David for his dancing before the ark, she was barren to the day of her death.
scriptures: So Michal let David down through a window: and he went, and fled, and escaped.
And as the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart.

Then David returned to bless his household. And Michal the daughter of Saul came out to meet David, and said, How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself!
Therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death.
corruption_summary: Michal is enlisted either as a feminist heroine silenced by a patriarchal narrator or as a mere shrew; the text is interested in neither, and names the sin exactly — she despised worship in her heart before she opened her mouth.
corruption_paragraphs: Two bad readings compete over Michal. The older one makes her a nag and stops there, which misses that Scripture first shows her risking her life for David and lying to her father's soldiers to do it. The newer one makes her a woman with a legitimate grievance — taken, given away, taken back — whose critique of a king's indecency is suppressed by a narrator writing for the winners. The text does not conceal her wrongs; it records the forced marriage and Phalti weeping behind her. What it also records is where the fault lay, and it locates it precisely: “she despised him in her heart” before she said a word, and what she despised was a man dancing before the LORD. The barrenness is not narrated as David's revenge; it is stated flatly, in the passive of divine action.

The living issue is her actual objection, which is a perennial one about worship. Michal's complaint is that the king lost his dignity in front of servant girls. David's answer accepts the charge and raises it: “I will yet be more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight” (2Sa 6:22). Worship in Scripture is not undignified — David wore the linen ephod, the ark came up by the ordinance he had learned the hard way after Uzzah — but it is self-forgetting, and the person most offended by it is usually the one calculating how it looks. Note also what David does not do: he does not improvise. The lawful way of carrying the ark and the whole-hearted joy of the man carrying it belong together. Reverence without joy is Michal; joy without reverence is Uzzah's cart.
roots_summary: Hebrew Mikal (H4324), Michal, from mi ka-'El, who is like God; bazah (H959), to despise; karar (H3769), to whirl or dance.
roots_lines: Hebrew Mikal (H4324) — Michal; probably a contraction of the question “who is like God?”
Hebrew bazah (H959) — to despise, hold in contempt; used of her heart, and of Esau's birthright.
Hebrew karar (H3769) — to whirl, to dance; David's motion before the ark.
Hebrew 'ephod bad — a linen ephod; the priestly garment the king wore that day.
Hebrew terap̄im (H8655) — teraphim, a household image; what Michal laid in the bed (1Sa 19:13).
usage: “Michal let David down through a window” — the escape that saved a king.
“She despised him in her heart” — the sin located before it was spoken.
“Had no child unto the day of her death” — a sentence stated without comment.

pos: n. (a Danite of Zorah, father of Samson — the man who asked to be taught how to raise the child before the child was born)
etymology: From Hebrew Manoach, “rest” or “resting place”, from nuach, to rest — the same root as Noah. It is an unexpected name for the father of the least restful man in the Old Testament.
biblical_def: Manoah is introduced in the plainest terms: “there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not” (Jdg 13:2). The angel of the LORD appeared to the wife, not to him, and told her she would conceive a Nazarite from the womb. Manoah's response is the finest thing recorded of him and one of the best prayers a father ever prayed: “Then Manoah intreated the LORD, and said, O my Lord, let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born” (Jdg 13:8). He did not ask for a sign, a fortune, or a guarantee; he asked for instruction in how to bring the boy up. God granted it, and the angel came again, and repeated what He had already said — the mother's diet, the child's vow — adding nothing, because the instruction had already been complete. When Manoah pressed for a name he was told it was secret, and when the flame went up from the altar and the angel went up in it, he fell on his face and said, “We shall surely die, because we have seen God” (Jdg 13:22). His wife reasoned him out of it. At the end of Samson's life his brethren carried him home and buried him “in the buryingplace of Manoah his father” (Jdg 16:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Manoah; in sacred history he is a man of Zorah, of the tribe of Dan, the father of Samson.
webster_full: MANOAH, n. A Danite of Zorah, the father of Samson; the name signifies rest.
His wife being barren, the angel of the Lord appeared to her and promised a son.
Manoah entreated that the man of God might come again and teach them how to order the child.
He offered a kid with a meat offering upon a rock unto the Lord, and the angel ascended in the flame.
Samson was buried in the buryingplace of Manoah his father, between Zorah and Eshtaol.
scriptures: Jdg 13:2
And there was a certain man of Zorah, of the family of the Danites, whose name was Manoah; and his wife was barren, and bare not.
Jdg 13:8
Then Manoah intreated the LORD, and said, O my Lord, let the man of God which thou didst send come again unto us, and teach us what we shall do unto the child that shall be born.
And Manoah said unto his wife, We shall surely die, because we have seen God.

Then his brethren and all the house of his father came down, and took him, and brought him up, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the buryingplace of Manoah his father. And he judged Israel twenty years.
corruption_summary: Parenting is treated as a matter of technique to be researched; Manoah asked God for the ordering of a child and received a repetition of what had already been revealed, because the instruction was already given.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the shape of God's answer to Jdg 13:8. Manoah wanted to be taught how to order the child, and God sent the messenger back, and the messenger said what he had said before and no more: let her beware of wine and unclean things and observe all that was commanded. There was no additional revelation because none was needed. The pattern holds for Christian parents, who are drowning in method and short on the one thing given: “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and the daily catechising of Deu 6:7 — talking of the words of God sitting in the house, walking by the way, lying down, rising up. The prayer was right and the answer was the word already spoken.

The second thing is the marriage, and it is quietly instructive. The angel came to the wife twice; Manoah had to ask to be included. She is the one who reasons clearly when he panics about dying — if the LORD were pleased to kill us, He would not have received an offering at our hands nor told us all this. She is the theologian in the house at that moment, and Scripture records it without embarrassment and without unsettling anything about the order of the home. Headship is not the claim that a husband is always the clearest thinker in the room. Manoah led his house to the altar; his wife steadied him when he was afraid; and the Holy Ghost wrote both down.
roots_summary: Hebrew Manoach (H4495), rest, from nuach (H5117), to rest; nazir (H5139), a Nazarite; mishpat (H4941), the manner or ordering.
roots_lines: Hebrew Manoach (H4495) — Manoah, “rest”; from the same root as the name Noah.
Hebrew nuach (H5117) — to rest, settle down; the word of the ark resting on Ararat.
Hebrew nazir (H5139) — a Nazarite, one separated by vow; Samson was one from the womb.
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, manner, ordering; “how shall we order the child?” (Jdg 13:12).
Hebrew pil'i (H6383) — wonderful, secret; the angel's answer about his name (Jdg 13:18), and a title of Christ in Isa 9:6.
usage: “His wife was barren, and bare not” — how a deliverer's story begins.
“Teach us what we shall do unto the child” — the prayer of a father before a birth.
“We shall surely die, because we have seen God” — fear answered by a wife's plain reasoning.

pos: n. (grandfather and brother of Abraham — the man who stayed in Mesopotamia, and whose city and daughters supplied the wives of the covenant line)
etymology: From Hebrew Nachor, probably from nachar, to snort or breathe hard, or from a root meaning to be scorched. Two men bear it: Terah's father and Terah's son, so Abraham had both a grandfather and a brother called Nahor.
biblical_def: Nahor is Abraham's brother, and he is the man who did not go. When the LORD said “Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house” (Gen 12:1), the family divided: Abram went, and Nahor stayed in Mesopotamia, where his household prospered and became a place on the map — the servant of Abraham “went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor” (Gen 24:10) to fetch a wife for Isaac, and found Rebekah at the well, granddaughter of Nahor by Milcah (Gen 11:29; Gen 22:20). A generation later Jacob went the same road for Rachel and Leah. So the wives of the patriarchs came from the branch that stayed behind, which kept the line clear of Canaan but did not keep it clear of idols: Rachel stole her father's teraphim, and when Jacob and Laban made their covenant at Mizpah, Laban swore by a plural — “The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us” (Gen 31:53) — and Jacob pointedly sware by the fear of his father Isaac instead. Joshua puts the matter beyond doubt at Shechem: Terah, “the father of Abraham, and the father of Nachor… served other gods” (Jos 24:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Nahor; in sacred history it names the grandfather of Abraham and also Abraham's brother, who dwelt in Mesopotamia.
webster_full: NAHOR, n. The son of Serug and father of Terah, and so the grandfather of Abraham.
Also, the son of Terah and brother of Abraham and Haran.
He married Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran, and had eight sons by her.
Bethuel his son was the father of Rebekah and of Laban.
The city of Nahor in Mesopotamia was the place whither Abraham's servant went to seek a wife for Isaac.
scriptures: And Abram and Nahor took them wives: the name of Abram's wife was Sarai; and the name of Nahor's wife, Milcah, the daughter of Haran, the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah.
And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying, Behold, Milcah, she hath also born children unto thy brother Nahor;
And the servant took ten camels of the camels of his master, and departed; for all the goods of his master were in his hand: and he arose, and went to Mesopotamia, unto the city of Nahor.
The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor, the God of their father, judge betwixt us. And Jacob sware by the fear of his father Isaac.
corruption_summary: Gen 31:53 is used to argue that the patriarchs were henotheists with tribal deities; Jacob's deliberate refusal of Laban's formula, and Joshua's testimony about Terah, show the text knows exactly what it is reporting.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments read Laban's oath — the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor judge between us — as evidence that Israel's religion evolved out of clan deities, one god per family, and only later became monotheism. The text itself defeats the reading, because it makes a point of Jacob's refusal to say it. Laban swears by a plural; Jacob swears by “the fear of his father Isaac”, singular and personal, declining to place Nahor's gods alongside his own. And Joshua tells Israel to their face what their ancestry was: on the other side of the flood, Terah served other gods. Scripture's account of its own origin is not that Abraham's family was pure and became more so; it is that God called one idolater out of an idolatrous house, which is what grace always does.

The second thing here is Nahor as the road not taken. He stayed where the family already was, and by every visible measure he did well: a city with his name on it, eight sons by Milcah, a prosperous house at Haran that could send caravans and marry daughters into wealth. Abraham lived in tents his whole life and owned one field with a cave in it. Hebrews explains the difference and it is not a difference of temperament: he “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10). Both brothers ended with a city. Only one of them was looking for the right one.
roots_summary: Hebrew Nachor (H5152), Nahor; Milkah (H4435), Milcah, queen; pachad Yitschaq, the fear of Isaac; terap̄im (H8655), household gods.
roots_lines: Hebrew Nachor (H5152) — Nahor; borne by Abraham's grandfather and by his brother.
Hebrew Milkah (H4435) — Milcah, “queen”; Nahor's wife and Rebekah's grandmother.
Hebrew Bethu'el (H1328) — Bethuel, their son, father of Rebekah and Laban.
Hebrew pachad (H6343) — dread, fear; “the fear of his father Isaac”, a divine title Jacob uses twice.
Hebrew 'Aram Naharayim — Mesopotamia, Aram of the two rivers; the country of the city of Nahor.
usage: “Abram and Nahor took them wives” — two brothers, two roads.
“Unto the city of Nahor” — where the covenant line went for its brides.
“The God of Abraham, and the God of Nahor” — a formula Jacob would not repeat.

pos: n. (Jesse's firstborn, passed over at the anointing of David — the tall man God refused, and the elder brother who despised the shepherd)
etymology: From Hebrew 'Eli'ab, “God is father”, from 'El, God, and 'ab, father. Several men bear it, including the prince of Zebulun in the wilderness and a Reubenite whose sons were swallowed with Korah.
biblical_def: Eliab was the eldest of Jesse's eight sons — “Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third” (1Ch 2:13) — and Scripture uses him twice to make the same point. When Samuel came to Bethlehem with the horn of oil, Eliab was brought first, and the prophet, who had spent a lifetime in the LORD's service, got it wrong on sight and said so. The answer given him is one of the most quoted verses in the Old Testament and one of the least believed: “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1Sa 16:7). The second occasion is the valley of Elah, where Eliab, standing in an army that had not moved for forty days, turned on his youngest brother for asking a question: “Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart” (1Sa 17:28). It is a perfect specimen of the accusation that describes the accuser. Eliab is not, however, cast off: his daughter Abihail married Rehoboam (2Ch 11:18), so his blood entered the royal line after all.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Eliab; in sacred history it is the name of the eldest son of Jesse, of a prince of Zebulun, and of a Reubenite in the time of Moses.
webster_full: ELIAB, n. A Hebrew name signifying God is father.
The eldest son of Jesse the Bethlehemite, and brother of David.
Samuel, seeing him, thought the Lord's anointed was before him, but the Lord refused him.
He served in the army of Saul, and was angry with David in the valley of Elah.
Eliab the son of Helon was prince of the tribe of Zebulun in the wilderness.
scriptures: And Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab, and Abinadab the second, and Shimma the third,

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.

And Eliab his eldest brother heard when he spake unto the men; and Eliab's anger was kindled against David, and he said, Why camest thou down hither? and with whom hast thou left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart; for thou art come down that thou mightest see the battle.
And Rehoboam took him Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David to wife, and Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse;
corruption_summary: 1Sa 16:7 is used to license indifference about outward conduct — God sees the heart, so the visible does not matter; the verse is about God's power to see what man cannot, not about the irrelevance of what man can.
corruption_paragraphs: “Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” is regularly deployed to mean that God is unconcerned with how a professing Christian looks, speaks, dresses, or behaves in public. That is a use the verse cannot bear. The point of contrast is not appearance versus reality but human blindness versus divine sight: Samuel could see a tall man and could not see a heart, and God could. Far from making the outward indifferent, Scripture insists that the heart eventually shows — “by their fruits ye shall know them” (Mat 7:20), and “out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh” (Mat 12:34). Eliab proved the diagnosis himself one chapter later, when the heart God had already refused came out of his mouth in the valley of Elah.

The second corruption is the flattening of Eliab into a mere foil. He was a soldier in a paralysed army, watching a giant blaspheme every morning for six weeks, and no doubt hating himself for it — and then his little brother arrived, asked what the reward was, and made everyone uncomfortable. His accusation, “I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart”, is a projection so exact that it functions as a confession. The temptation is a common one in the church: the man who will not act resents the man who does, and dresses the resentment as discernment about the other man's motives. David's reply is the model — “Is there not a cause?” — and then he turned away from him to someone else and got on with it.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'Eli'ab (H446), from 'El (H410), God, and 'ab (H1), father; ra'ah (H7200), to see; lebab (H3824), the heart.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'Eli'ab (H446) — Eliab, “God is father”; borne by Jesse's firstborn and others.
Hebrew ra'ah (H7200) — to see, to look at; used three times in 1Sa 16:7, of man's sight and God's.
Hebrew 'enayim — the eyes; the Hebrew of “outward appearance” is literally “to the eyes”.
Hebrew lebab (H3824) — the heart; in Hebrew the seat of mind, will, and affection together, not the emotions alone.
Hebrew ma'as (H3988) — to reject, refuse; “I have refused him”, the same verb used of Saul in 1Sa 15:23.
usage: “Jesse begat his firstborn Eliab” — the son everyone would have chosen.
“The LORD looketh on the heart” — the reason he was passed by.
“I know thy pride, and the naughtiness of thine heart” — an accusation that named its author.

pos: n. (second son of Canaan and ancestor of the Hittites — whose children sold Abraham a grave, and whose daughters grieved Isaac and Rebekah)
etymology: From Hebrew Cheth, of uncertain meaning; a terror or a dread has been suggested from chathath, to be shattered or dismayed. The same consonant is the name of the eighth Hebrew letter.
biblical_def: Heth is a man, second in the list of Canaan's sons — “Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth” (Gen 10:15) — and Scripture speaks of his posterity in a distinctive way. Where other nations get a gentilic, Heth's people are repeatedly called “the children of Heth” and “the sons of Heth”, as though the family were still felt in the nation. They appear at their best in Genesis 23. Sarah has died at Hebron, and Abraham, who owns nothing, comes to them: “Abraham stood up from before his dead, and spake unto the sons of Heth” (Gen 23:3), and again, “Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth” (Gen 23:7). They offer him the choicest sepulchre free; he insists on paying full weight for the field of Machpelah, in public, at the gate, and so acquires the only land he ever owned in the country God had given him. They appear at their worst in the next generation, not by any act of theirs but by marriage: “Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth” (Gen 27:46) — the two Hittite wives Esau had taken. That sentence is what sent Jacob to Padanaram, and so, humanly speaking, the daughters of Heth set the whole second half of Genesis in motion.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no article for Heth; in sacred history he is the second son of Canaan, from whom descended the Hittites, called in Genesis the children of Heth.
webster_full: HETH, n. The second son of Canaan, the son of Ham.
From him descended the Hittites, who are frequently called the sons or children of Heth.
They dwelt about Hebron, and of them Abraham bought the field and cave of Machpelah.
Esau took two of the daughters of Heth to wife, which was a grief of mind to Isaac and Rebekah.
Heth is also the name of the eighth letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
scriptures: And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,
Gen 23:3
And Abraham stood up from before his dead, and spake unto the sons of Heth, saying,
Gen 23:7
And Abraham stood up, and bowed himself to the people of the land, even to the children of Heth.

And Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?
corruption_summary: Abraham's insistence on paying four hundred shekels is read as oriental haggling etiquette; the text presents it as faith refusing to hold the promised land on any title but God's gift and an honest purchase.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover from the sons of Heth is Abraham's conduct at their gate. He was offered the grave for nothing by a people who called him “a mighty prince among us”, and he refused, weighed out four hundred shekels of silver “current money with the merchant”, and had the transaction witnessed by everyone who went in at the gate. He would not have the burial place of the covenant on a Canaanite's favour, and he would not take advantage of the courtesy of grief. Christians conducting business with unbelievers might read the chapter as a manual: full price, public terms, no leaning on goodwill, nothing that could later be called a debt.

The second thing is the grave itself, and it is the reason Genesis spends a whole chapter on a property deed. Abraham had been promised the land and owned none of it; the one parcel he acquired he bought to bury a body in, and he, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob were all laid there. It is the most eloquent act of faith in Genesis. A man who believed the land was his descendants' but expected to die first put his wife into the ground of it as a stake, and Hebrews says of that whole company that they “died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off” (Heb 11:13). Buying a grave in a country you have been promised is a confession of resurrection.
roots_summary: Hebrew Cheth (H2845), Heth; Chitti (H2850), Hittite; Makpelah (H4375), Machpelah, a doubling.
roots_lines: Hebrew Cheth (H2845) — Heth; second son of Canaan in the table of nations.
Hebrew bene-Cheth — “the children of Heth”; the phrase used ten times in Gen 23 alone.
Hebrew Makpelah (H4375) — Machpelah, from kaphal, to double; the double cave Abraham bought.
Hebrew keseph 'ober la-socher — “current money with the merchant”; Abraham paid in trade-weight silver (Gen 23:16).
Hebrew nasi' 'Elohim — “a mighty prince”, literally a prince of God; what they called him (Gen 23:6).
usage: “Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth” — a name in the table of nations.
“Abraham… bowed himself… even to the children of Heth” — a patriarch buying a grave.
“I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth” — the sentence that sent Jacob east.

pos: n. (the second son of Noah — father of Cush, Mizraim, Phut, and Canaan, and the man whose sin brought a curse on one branch of his line)
etymology: From Hebrew Cham, probably “hot” or “burnt”, from a root meaning warmth; the poetic name for Egypt in the Psalms is “the land of Ham”. It should not be confused with the letter or with the several place-names of similar sound.
biblical_def: Ham is one of the three sons of Noah who came through the flood, and from him descend the peoples of Africa and of Canaan: “the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan” (Gen 10:6). Egypt is called the land of Ham in the psalms — “Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham” (Psa 105:23). The episode that defines him took place after the flood in a vineyard. Noah drank of the wine and was uncovered in his tent, and “Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without” (Gen 9:22). Shem and Japheth took a garment, laid it on their shoulders, walked backward, and covered him without looking. When Noah awoke he pronounced a word that has been quarrelled over ever since — and its object is precise: “Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren” (Gen 9:25). Not Ham. Not Cush, Mizraim, or Phut. Canaan, the one branch of Ham's house that would occupy the land God had promised Abraham, and whose iniquity Gen 15:16 says would be measured and filled. The curse was fulfilled in the conquest, and again when Solomon put the Canaanite remnant to bond-service.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives Ham as the youngest son of Noah, and notes that in Scripture Egypt is called the land of Ham.
webster_full: HAM, n. The son of Noah, and father of Cush, Mizraim, Phut and Canaan.
The name signifies hot or burnt, and his posterity peopled Africa and the southern regions.
Egypt is in the Psalms called the land of Ham.
Seeing his father's nakedness, he told his brethren, who covered Noah, going backward.
The curse pronounced by Noah upon awaking fell upon Canaan, the son of Ham.
scriptures: Gen 9:22
And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without.
Gen 9:25
And he said, Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren.
Gen 10:6
And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan.
Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham.
corruption_summary: The “curse of Ham” was invented to justify the enslavement of Africans; the text curses Canaan, not Ham, names no colour, and was fulfilled in the conquest of a Levantine people.
corruption_paragraphs: This is one of the worst misreadings in the history of the church, and it must be named plainly. From the medieval period and with great force in the Atlantic slave trade, Gen 9:25 was preached as a divine warrant for the perpetual bondage of black Africans — the so-called curse of Ham. Every step of the argument is false. The curse is pronounced on Canaan and is repeated three times as Canaan; Ham's other sons, including Cush, are not mentioned in it. Skin colour appears nowhere in the passage or anywhere near it. The Canaanites were a Levantine people, and the curse was discharged in the conquest under Joshua and in the bond-service of the remnant under Solomon. And Scripture's doctrine of man forbids the conclusion in advance: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men” (Act 17:26), every human being bears the image of God (Gen 1:27), and manstealing is a capital crime under the law — “he that stealeth a man, and selleth him… he shall surely be put to death” (Exo 21:16), with the man-stealer named in Paul's list of the lawless in 1Ti 1:10. The dictionary holds that the texts were not misunderstood so much as pressed into service, and that the men who did it were condemned by the same Bible they quoted.

The second thing in the passage, and the one usually lost in the argument, is what Shem and Japheth did. Their brother published their father's shame; they walked backward with a garment on their shoulders and would not look. It is the Old Testament's picture of what love does with another man's disgrace — “charity shall cover the multitude of sins” (1Pe 4:8), and “he that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth very friends” (Pro 17:9). Noah's sin is not excused by the narrative; he is drunk and uncovered and the record stands. But the sons are judged by what they did with a father's nakedness, and the one who told is the one whose line was cursed.
roots_summary: Hebrew Cham (H2526), Ham, hot; Kena'an (H3667), Canaan; 'ebed 'abadim, a servant of servants; 'erwah (H6172), nakedness.
roots_lines: Hebrew Cham (H2526) — Ham; second or youngest son of Noah, father of four nations.
Hebrew Kena'an (H3667) — Canaan; Ham's fourth son, and the only one named in the curse.
Hebrew 'ebed 'abadim — “a servant of servants”; a Hebrew superlative, the lowest of servants.
Hebrew 'erwah (H6172) — nakedness, shame; the word of the Leviticus laws on family shame.
Hebrew kasah (H3680) — to cover, conceal; what Shem and Japheth did, and what love does (Pro 10:12).
usage: “Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father” — a sin of publishing.
“Cursed be Canaan” — the curse falls on one named son, and not on Ham.
“Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham” — Egypt named for its ancestor.

pos: n. (worthlessness — a Hebrew abstract noun used of the lawless, and by Paul as a name for Satan himself)
etymology: From Hebrew Beliya'al, most likely from beli, without, and ya'al, profit or use — hence worthlessness, that which yields nothing. An older suggestion reads it “without going up”, that is, one who never rises. The KJV keeps the Hebrew as a proper name rather than translating it.
biblical_def: Belial is not, in the Old Testament, the name of a demon; it is a Hebrew noun meaning worthlessness, and it is nearly always found in the phrases “sons of Belial”, “children of Belial”, or “a man of Belial”. What the phrase describes is a very particular kind of wickedness — not weakness or ignorance but a settled lawlessness that recognises no authority. The instances are ugly and consistent. The mob at Gibeah: “certain sons of Belial beset the house round about, and beat at the door” (Jdg 19:22). The priesthood at Shiloh: “the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD” (1Sa 2:12). Abigail on her husband: “this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he” (1Sa 25:25). The rebel who split the kingdom: “there happened to be there a man of Belial, whose name was Sheba, the son of Bichri” (2Sa 20:1). The false witnesses who killed Naboth were sons of Belial too. By the intertestamental period the word had hardened into a personal name for the evil one, and Paul uses it that way, exactly once, in a passage forbidding covenant fellowship with unbelief: “And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” (2Co 6:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Belial as a Hebrew word signifying wickedness or worthlessness, and notes that sons of Belial denotes wicked, worthless men, and that Paul uses it of Satan.
webster_full: BELIAL, n. As a Hebrew word, it signifies unprofitableness, wickedness, worthlessness.
In Scripture, sons or men of Belial are lawless, worthless, wicked men.
It is compounded of beli, without, and yaal, profit or usefulness.
The word is used in the New Testament as a name of Satan, the adversary: what concord hath Christ with Belial?
It denotes not weakness merely, but a settled refusal of all yoke and authority.
scriptures: Now as they were making their hearts merry, behold, the men of the city, certain sons of Belial, beset the house round about, and beat at the door, and spake to the master of the house, the old man, saying, Bring forth the man that came into thine house, that we may know him.
Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.

Let not my lord, I pray thee, regard this man of Belial, even Nabal: for as his name is, so is he; Nabal is his name, and folly is with him: but I thine handmaid saw not the young men of my lord, whom thou didst send.
And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?
corruption_summary: Wickedness is redefined as damage or dysfunction, categories that call for treatment; Belial names it as worthlessness before God — a moral and not a therapeutic verdict.
corruption_paragraphs: The word Belial cuts directly across the modern moral vocabulary, which is why it sounds so strange now. Contemporary language for evil is drawn from medicine and injury: behaviour is unhealthy, damaging, or the product of unmet need, and the remedy is treatment and understanding. Scripture's category here is different in kind. Beliya'al is a verdict of worthlessness — a man who yields no profit, who has thrown off the yoke, who “knew not the LORD”. The men of Gibeah were not unwell; the sons of Eli were not under-resourced. The Bible does have deep compassion for the afflicted, and it distinguishes carefully between the sinned-against and the sinner. But it will not let the distinction dissolve the category of the wicked, because a man who cannot be called wicked cannot be called to repent, and a doctrine of sin is the only ground on which forgiveness can be offered.

The other thing to hold is the phrase Paul quarries out of it. 2Co 6:15 sits in the passage that begins “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers”, and the argument is a series of questions with only one answer: righteousness with unrighteousness, light with darkness, Christ with Belial, the temple of God with idols. Paul is not forbidding contact with unbelievers — he had already told the same church that this would require going out of the world. He is forbidding the yoke: the binding partnership, the shared enterprise, the marriage, in which a believer's course is tied to an unbeliever's. The old Hebrew word for a man with no yoke turns up in the New Testament to warn believers about the yokes they choose.
roots_summary: Hebrew Beliya'al (H1100), worthlessness, from beli (H1097), without, and ya'al (H3276), to profit; Greek Belial (G955).
roots_lines: Hebrew Beliya'al (H1100) — Belial; worthlessness, destruction, wickedness.
Hebrew beli (H1097) — without, failure, nothing; the negative particle in the compound.
Hebrew ya'al (H3276) — to profit, to be of use; the second element, giving “good for nothing”.
Hebrew ben-Beliya'al — “son of Belial”; a Hebrew idiom of character, as “son of peace” or “sons of thunder”.
Greek Belial (G955) — Belial; used once, of Satan, in 2Co 6:15.
usage: “Certain sons of Belial beset the house” — the mob at Gibeah.
“The sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD” — the verdict on a priesthood.
“What concord hath Christ with Belial?” — a question with only one answer.
